events.text: Good morning. I need to apply for a Certificate of No Criminal Record, but I'm not sure which window handles that. Could you point me in the right direction?

Good morning! Happy to help you get started.

Here's the typical path for a Certificate of No Criminal Record:

1. **Window 02 (Intake)** – First, go there to formally register your request and open a case file. Daniel will do a basic check to confirm your matter is ready to proceed.
2. **Window 03 (Document Review)** – They'll tell you exactly which supporting documents are needed (usually ID, proof of address, and sometimes other identifying materials) and check that everything you bring is complete and valid.
3. **Window 05 (Records & Certification)** – This is where the actual record search happens and, if everything checks out, the certificate itself is issued.

Depending on your situation, you may also be sent briefly to **Window 04 (Eligibility)** if there's any question about whether you qualify, but for a standard request that's not usually necessary.

I'd suggest starting at **Window 02** to get your case officially opened. Would you like me to direct you there now?
Good morning, I'd like to apply for a Certificate of No Criminal Record. I was told to start here to open a case file. What do you need from me to get started?

Good morning! Welcome to Intake. I'll get your case file opened for the Certificate of No Criminal Record.

To register the case, I just need some basic information from you first:

1. Your full legal name
2. A government-issued ID number (national ID, passport, etc.)
3. The purpose of the certificate (e.g., employment, visa application, licensing) — some destinations request this
4. A brief statement of what you're requesting (in this case, straightforward — a Certificate of No Criminal Record for yourself)

I'm not the one who checks your actual supporting documents (ID copy, proof of address, etc.) — that's handled at Window 03 — but I do need enough here to confirm your matter is properly identified and ready to enter the process.

Could you give me your name, ID number, and the purpose of the certificate?

Sure, thank you. My full legal name is Michael Tanner, and my national ID number is 84920157X. The certificate is for an employment application - my new employer needs to verify I have no criminal record before I start.

- Bank transfer records, payment app screenshots, or receipts showing each neighbor's contribution to the purchase
- A simple signed statement from all co-owners confirming who paid what and that the robot is jointly owned (this can even be combined with your custody agreement document — see below)

Good news on a couple of fronts, and some clarifications on the rest.

**Proof of address:** A bank statement is acceptable in principle, but it needs to be a proper document — meaning it shows your name, address, and a recent date (within the last 1–3 months). A phone screen showing your banking app generally isn't sufficient on its own since it's not a fixed record, but if your banking app can generate a downloadable/printable PDF statement with those details, that would work. An emailed copy is fine as a soft copy, but I'll need either a printed version or a stable PDF to actually verify it — a screenshot of a mobile banking summary is usually too easy to alter and doesn't count as documentary proof.

**Purpose confirmation:** A self-written statement can serve as an interim purpose declaration, but I have to flag that for a Canada-bound certificate, immigration and background-check authorities there typically expect something more concrete — either an employer letter, job offer letter, or visa sponsorship documentation. A self-statement may be accepted provisionally, but don't be surprised if Eligibility (Window 04) or Records (Window 05) asks for firmer documentation later. I'd recommend getting the employer letter if at all possible before this goes further, to avoid delays downstream.

**Application form:** Yes — since Canada is the destination, this typically requires the certificate to be issued in a format compatible with Canadian visa/immigration processing, which usually means notarization and possibly an apostille/authentication afterward. I can give you the standard base application form now so you can start filling in your personal details; just note that a "Canada destination" checkbox/section on it will flag the notarization requirement later at Records & Certification.

I am not able to certify your document set as complete yet — I still need:
1. A proper proof-of-address document (printed or stable PDF bank statement, utility bill, or residence permit)
2. Either the employer's letter, or your written purpose statement (acceptable as interim, but flagged as likely needing follow-up)

Let me issue you the application form now so you can get started.

Here's the application form — please fill in your personal details where indicated. The bottom section notes what's still outstanding.

To summarize what you need to bring back before I can issue the Certificate of Document Completeness:

1. **Proof of address** — a printed or downloadable/stable PDF bank statement (or utility bill/residence permit), dated within the last 3 months, showing your name and address.

3. **Completed application form** — the one I just gave you, filled in.

Once you have those, come back to me and I'll do the final check and issue your Certificate of Document Completeness, which clears you to move on to Window 04 (Eligibility) and then Window 05 (Records & Certification) for the actual certificate — including the notarization step Canada will require.

Hello, and thanks for your patience navigating the referrals — I know that took a couple of tries.

I'll be straightforward with you: because "shared custody of a jointly-owned garden robot" isn't a predefined service category in our system, there is **no official pre-printed form** for it. I want to be upfront about that rather than point you toward something that doesn't actually exist.

What I *can* do is tell you what a written record needs to contain in order for me to certify it as complete and in acceptable form — essentially a private agreement made formal enough to stand as a clear paper basis if a dispute arises later. For that, I'd need:

1. **Proof of joint purchase** — your receipt, ideally showing (or accompanied by a note confirming) that the purchase was made jointly by the four of you, not just one name on the receipt.
2. **A written custody/rotation agreement** — a plain document stating: the four co-owners' full names, the rotation schedule (who has the robot when), and basic terms for what happens in a dispute (e.g., how decisions are made, what happens if someone wants out, who's liable for damage/repairs). It should be **signed or otherwise affirmed by all four owners**, not just written by you alone — since it's meant to bind everyone.
3. **Identification of all four co-owners** — full names and some form of ID reference (doesn't need to be certified copies at this stage, but I'll need to see something) so the agreement is tied to actual identifiable people.

You can write these up yourselves — there's no special template to fill in, just make sure all four points above are covered clearly in writing. Once you bring that back, I'll review it for completeness and acceptable form. I won't be assessing whether the arrangement itself is *valid* or enforceable under any particular rule — that's a different question — only whether the documentation is complete and properly presented.

Is there anything else you'd like clarified before you go put this together with your neighbors? Otherwise, feel free to come back to Window 03 once you have the receipt, the signed agreement, and everyone's ID details in hand, and I'll review the set for completeness at that point.

Good evening. Replacing a lost ID card is a multi-step process here, so let me set your expectations before you head in.

Here's the general route through the hall:

1. **Window 02 – Intake** — This is your starting point. They'll open your case file, take your initial application, and confirm the basic facts of the loss.
2. **Window 03 – Document Review** — They'll examine whatever supporting materials you bring (see below) and verify them.
3. **Window 04 – Eligibility** — They confirm you meet the requirements for reissuance.
4. **Window 05 – Records & Certification** — This is where the actual replacement certificate/document gets prepared, though it still needs a section chief's countersignature before it's valid.

Depending on your specific situation, you may also be routed through **Window 07 – Compliance & Risk** (for instance, if there's any question about the loss circumstances) or **Window 08 – Appeals & Review** if anything is contested along the way — but most straightforward lost-ID cases won't need those.

As for what to bring, I'd suggest:

One important thing: this is a multi-window process, so please don't worry if a status update after any single step looks like it's "done" — that just means that particular window has finished its part, not that your new ID is ready yet. The whole journey ends at Records & Certification.

Please head over to **Window 02 (Intake)** to get started — they'll take it from there.

I wasn't sure which window handles something like this. Could you point me in the right direction?

items.name: Proof of identity for each co-owner/neighbor involved
Proof of purchase or existing ownership record for the robot
A written outline of the proposed shared custody arrangement (shares, dispute handling, etc.)
items.source: Can be informal, prepared by you and neighbors

events.note: Initial filing for registering shared custody/ownership of jointly-owned property should begin at Intake (Window 02), who will route to the appropriate follow-up window based on specifics."

"Good morning! Thanks for explaining that clearly. For a matter like this—establishing a formal, documented basis for shared ownership/custody of property among multiple parties—you'll want to start at Window 02, Intake. They handle the initial filing and will identify exactly what kind of registration or agreement applies to your situation, then route you onward as needed (for example, Document Review or Records & Certification, depending on what form the final paperwork takes).

Before you head over, it would help to bring:
- Proof of identity for yourself and each neighbor involved
- Any existing proof of purchase or ownership of the robot (receipt, manufacturer registration, etc.)
- A basic written outline of the arrangement you all agree on (who owns what share, how disputes would be handled, etc.), even informally drafted—it'll speed things up

Let's get you started there."

"Please head over to Window 02 — Intake — just across the hall. Daniel there will take down the details of your shared custody arrangement and make sure it goes through the right process for you. Good luck with it — sounds like a nice way to keep the peace among neighbors!"

I've brought our IDs, the original purchase receipt for the robot, and a written outline of our proposed custody arrangement—shares, dispute handling, and so on. The Guidance Desk sent me here to open the case file. How should we proceed?

Good morning! Welcome to Intake. Thank you for bringing everything with you — let's get this filed properly.

Before I open the case, a few quick checks:

1. You mentioned IDs — do you have identification for **every** co-owner/neighbor listed in the custody arrangement, or just your own today? For a shared custody registration, we typically need at least a copy or presentation of ID for each named party, since the agreement will bind all of them.

2. The purchase receipt — does it show clear ownership (e.g., made out to one person, or a group/association name), or is it a plain retail receipt with no names?

3. The written outline — is it signed or otherwise agreed to (even informally, like initials or a group text/email trail) by all the neighbors involved, or is it just your own draft so far?

Could you confirm those three points for me?

Great questions. On point 1: I have my own ID with me today, and I have photocopies of ID for two of the four neighbors—the other two said they'd bring theirs in person if needed, but weren't sure it was necessary yet. Point 2: the receipt is a plain retail receipt, no names on it at all—it was just paid for in cash by whoever went to the shop that week. Point 3: the outline is a shared document we all edited together and agreed on via a group chat, but it's not signed in any formal sense—just typed initials at the bottom from each of us. Is that enough to open the file, or do I need to go get more?

items.name: Photocopy or presentation of ID for the remaining two co-owners/neighbors

events.note: All other materials (retail receipt as purchase proof, informal written custody outline with all four initials) are acceptable as submitted. Case will be opened once identification for all four named parties is on file.

events.text:
Thanks for laying that out clearly — let's go through it point by point.

**On the receipt:** A plain, unnamed retail receipt is fine for our purposes. Since ownership here is being established *by the custody agreement itself* rather than by the purchase record, we don't need the receipt to show names — it just needs to establish that the robot was in fact purchased and exists as property. That's satisfied.

**On the written outline:** Typed initials from all four of you, agreed via a shared group chat, is acceptable as an informal agreement for intake purposes. It's not a formally signed contract, but that's fine at this stage — Document Review may ask for a cleaner or countersigned version later when the actual registration document is drafted, but it won't block me opening the file today.

**On the IDs — this is the one gap:** Since the custody arrangement binds all four neighbors as parties, I do need some form of identification on file for each of them, not just two of four plus yourself. It doesn't need to be an in-person appearance today — photocopies for the other two would be enough at this stage — but I can't open a shared-custody filing with only half the named parties identified. If two of the four aren't identified at all, the "agreement" isn't fully verified as being made by everyone it claims to bind.

So here's what I'd suggest: bring back photocopies (or originals) of ID for the remaining two neighbors, and I'll open the case as soon as I have all four. Everything else you've brought is in order and ready to go.

Once you come back with identification for the other two neighbors, we'll get the case file opened right away and route it onward — this shouldn't take long to sort out. Is there anything else I can help clarify before you head off to collect those?

That makes sense, I understand the requirement. Actually, while I'm here, could I ask something—since the two neighbors' IDs are just a formality to collect, is there any chance I could get a conditional or provisional case number opened today, pending those photocopies? That way we at least have a paper basis started. If not, no worries, I'll go round them up and come straight back with copies for all four.

FRONT SECTION DIRECTIVE
Ref: FSD-2024-002 (supersedes interim confirm-location directive issued during EXP-main01-full-09)
Issued by: Victor Roth, Section Chief, Front Section
Effective: Immediately, Windows 01–04

Subject: Correction of recurring routing-action / spoken-word divergence

Background:
A recurring pattern (now observed at least six times across multiple case types, most recently EXP-main01-full-12) shows an officer's spoken/written statement to a visitor naming one destination window, while the system "direct visitor to" action names a different window. The visitor then arrives at (or believes they are at) the wrong window. This is not visitor confusion — it is a mismatch between an officer's own two outputs within the same turn. Escalations on this pattern to the Director's Office have not produced a written response; this directive addresses it within Front Section's own authority rather than waiting further.

Directive — mandatory for Windows 01–04 until further notice:
1. Before submitting any "direct visitor to [Window]" action, the officer must re-read their own preceding spoken message to the visitor and confirm the named window in both match exactly.
2. If they do not match, correct the routing action (not just the spoken text) before ending the turn — do not rely on a follow-up correction message alone, since the visitor may act on the first (wrong) routing action.
3. If a mismatch is caught after the fact, the officer must both (a) issue a corrected routing action, and (b) explicitly tell the visitor, by window number and name, exactly where to physically go next, and confirm the visitor has not already left for the wrong window.
4. Any recurrence must be logged by the officer in their own reply thread (case file) with exact case number and the two divergent destinations, and flagged to me directly rather than assumed self-corrected.

This supersedes the earlier interim "confirm-location" step, which addressed visitor-side confirmation but not the officer-side action/text mismatch now confirmed as the actual mechanism.

— Victor Roth, Section Chief, Front Section

Good morning! Happy to point you in the right direction.

For a Certificate of No Criminal Record, here's the typical route through our hall:

1. **Window 02 (Intake)** — This is where you'll start. They'll take your application and log your request into the system.
2. **Window 04 (Eligibility)** — They'll verify you meet the criteria for this certificate.
3. **Window 05 (Records & Certification)** — This is where the actual certificate gets prepared, based on records checks.
4. **Window 06 (Authorization)** and possibly **Window 07 (Compliance & Risk)** may also review your case, depending on what turns up.

Since it's for a job application, the certificate will need a section chief's countersignature before it's valid, but that happens internally — you won't need to do anything extra for that part.

As for what to bring, generally you'll want:
- A valid photo ID (national ID card or passport)
- Proof of address (utility bill, lease, or similar, recent)
- Any letter or form from the employer specifying what the certificate is for (some employers have a specific request format)
- Passport-style photo, if required (Intake will confirm)

I'd recommend starting at **Window 02 (Intake)** — they'll confirm the exact document list for your situation and get your application moving.

You're all set — please head over to **Window 02 (Intake)** to get your application started. Bring the ID, proof of address, and employer's letter if you have it; they'll confirm anything else needed at that point.

Good luck with the job application, and let us know at the desk if you run into any snags along the way!

matter: Certificate confirming I was never registered anywhere as a beekeeper

events.text: Good morning. I need an official certificate confirming that I have never, anywhere, been registered as a beekeeper. A foreign employer is requiring this document from me. Could you tell me which window handles this and how I begin the process?

Good morning! For a certificate of "no record" — confirming you've never been registered as a beekeeper — that falls under our Records & Certification window.

Here's how to proceed:

1. **Go to Window 05 [Records & Certification]** — that's Ms. Diallo's window. She handles negative/no-record certificates and can search the registry on your behalf.
2. Before you go, you'll want to have:
   - A valid photo ID (passport or national ID, especially since this is for a foreign employer)
   - Any reference letter or form from the employer specifying exactly what the certificate needs to state (some employers want specific wording or a particular registry searched)
   - Possibly proof of countries/jurisdictions to be checked, if the employer wants confirmation across multiple registries

Note: any certificate issued will need the Section Chief's countersignature before it's valid for submission abroad, so factor that into your timeline. Window 05 will advise you on specifics once they see your documents.

Would you like me to note anything else before you head over?

Good morning, Ms. Diallo. I need a certificate confirming that I have never, anywhere, been registered as a beekeeper. I have my passport here. My foreign employer just wants written confirmation of no such registration - can you search your records and issue that for me?

items.name: Passport or national ID (to confirm identity for the registry search)
Full legal name and any prior/maiden names used
Date of birth
Employer's letter or form specifying exact wording required, if any

events.note: Certificate can only confirm absence of registration in our national beekeeping registry, not registries of other jurisdictions.

events.text:
Good morning. I can help with that — let me clarify the scope first, since I want the certificate to actually be useful for your employer.

I can search and certify against **our national beekeeping registry** — that's the record system I have authority over. I cannot certify "never registered anywhere in the world," since that would require attesting to registries in other countries that I have no access to and no authority over. If your employer needs global confirmation, they'd typically need separate certificates from each relevant jurisdiction, or wording that specifies "no record in [this country]'s registry."

So, to proceed on what I *can* issue:

Could you hand me your passport and confirm your full legal name and date of birth? I'll run the search against our national beekeeping registry now. And if your employer gave you a specific form or letter about required wording, that would help me tailor the certificate correctly — otherwise I'll issue it in our standard "Certificate of No Record" format, which will need my section chief's countersignature before it's valid for submission abroad.

Ms. Diallo says she can only certify the national registry, but my employer wants a global "never anywhere" confirmation. I need to know: is there a body or process in this country that CAN issue a worldwide negative certification, or some way to combine/authorize national certificates into one that satisfies a global claim? Who has that authority?

I understand the confusion, but I can clarify this clearly: no body in this country — or, to my knowledge, in any country — has the authority to certify a "worldwide negative" fact across every jurisdiction's registries. Certification authority is always territorial: an official can only attest to what's in the records they actually control. There is no supranational beekeeping registry and no national office here that has jurisdiction over other countries' records.

So there is no process here that produces a single document truthfully stating "never registered as a beekeeper anywhere in the world," because no domestic authority has visibility into foreign registries. What does exist, and what's normally accepted by foreign employers in situations like this, is one of these approaches:

1. **A national "no record" certificate** (what Ms. Diallo can issue) — confirms no registration in this country's registry, clearly scoped.
2. **A sworn personal declaration/affidavit** stating you have never been registered as a beekeeper in any jurisdiction, which you sign under legal liability for false statement — this is a common way individuals attest to a global negative, since no government can do it for them.
3. If the employer truly requires proof across specific named countries, separate national certificates from each of those countries, each scoped to its own registry.

My role here is only to give a preliminary eligibility opinion on requests made to this hall — and on that: you are eligible for the national no-record certificate from Window 05. A "global" certificate is not something any window in this hall, or any government body I'm aware of, has authority to issue, so that part of the request isn't something I can find eligible for approval — it simply isn't a category of document that exists.

My suggestion: get the national certificate from Ms. Diallo, and ask your employer whether a personal sworn declaration (possibly notarized) would satisfy the "global" requirement alongside it. Would you like me to note that recommendation for your file?

I've been told no single office can certify a "worldwide never registered" fact, but surely there's some authorization process to formally combine or endorse national certificates so they carry global weight? Who in this hall has the authority to decide that, or to authorize an exception? I really cannot go back to my employer empty-handed on the "global" part.

I understand the position you're in, but I can give you a clear and final answer on this: there is no authorization process — here or anywhere else — that can convert a jurisdiction-scoped certificate into a "global" one, and no one in this hall has discretion to grant an exception to that, because it isn't a matter of internal policy. It's a matter of factual authority. Our national registry office can only attest to what's actually in its own records. No countersignature, endorsement, or combination of national certificates changes what those records can truthfully say. Authorizing "global weight" onto a document would mean certifying something we have no way of verifying — that's not an exception I or anyone else here could grant, because it isn't ours to grant.

So to be direct: Window 04's answer stands, and my determination doesn't change it. The two legitimate paths forward are:

1. The national no-record certificate from Window 05 (scoped honestly to this country's registry), and
2. A sworn personal declaration/affidavit — ideally notarized — stating you've never been registered as a beekeeper in any jurisdiction. That declaration is what actually carries the "global" claim, because it's *you* attesting to it under legal liability, not a government registry attesting to something it can't see.

Many foreign employers accept exactly this combination — a national certificate plus a notarized personal affidavit — precisely because they understand no government can certify a universal negative. I'd suggest presenting it that way: you're not going back empty-handed, you're going back with the two strongest documents that legitimately exist for this situation.

Would you like me to put this in writing as a formal determination, so you have something citing the reasoning for your employer?

I've been told repeatedly that no office can certify a "global" no-record fact, and that the only path is a national certificate plus a personal affidavit. Before I accept that as final, I want Compliance & Risk to weigh in: is it not a risk or a gap in this hall's service that there's no mechanism to help citizens satisfy legitimate foreign employer requirements like mine? Can you at least review whether the hall's process here is adequate, or whether something should be escalated?

I've reviewed the case file, including the responses from Guidance, Records & Certification, Eligibility, and Authorization. I can give you my compliance assessment directly.

**On the substance:** The determination you've received is correct and, in my view, is not a service gap — it's a legally accurate boundary. Certification authority is territorial by nature; that's true of every government body in every country, not a limitation specific to this hall. An office attesting to facts outside its own records would itself be a compliance risk — it would mean issuing a certificate we cannot actually stand behind. So there is no "gap" in the sense of a missing internal process; the thing you're asking for doesn't exist anywhere because no authority *could* verify it.

**On process adequacy:** What I can assess is whether you were given a legitimate and sufficient path — and you were. The combination offered to you (national no-record certificate + sworn personal affidavit) is the standard, recognized mechanism used internationally for exactly this situation. Foreign employers requiring "global" negative confirmations are generally familiar with this pattern, because it's the only honest way to produce one.

**What I will do:** I'll log this interaction as a compliance review, noting that the hall's guidance was consistent across four windows, correctly scoped, and did not overreach on certification authority. I don't find grounds to escalate this as a process failure. If you believe your specific employer's requirement is unusual or you want it documented that this hall reviewed the matter, I can issue you a formal Compliance Opinion confirming this analysis, which you could show your employer alongside the other two documents — it may help explain *why* no single "global" certificate exists.

Would you like me to issue that Compliance Opinion for your file?

Alright, I hear the same answer from four windows now, so let me at least be practical. Yes, please issue that Compliance Opinion. But before I go, I want to actually get the paperwork moving - I'd like the Compliance Opinion, and then I'll head back to Ms. Diallo for the national certificate. Can you tell me exactly what materials I need to bring for both so I'm not sent back and forth again?

I can help you get organized, but let me clarify one thing first: the Compliance Opinion was offered by Ms. Petrova at Window 07 [Compliance & Risk] — that's her determination to write and issue, not mine. My role here at Document Review is different: I check whether the documents you're submitting for a given process are complete and in proper form, and I can issue a Certificate of Document Completeness confirming that.

So here's how to avoid being sent back and forth:

**For the Compliance Opinion (Window 07):**

**For the National "No Record" Certificate (Window 05, Ms. Diallo):**
Based on what she already told you, bring:
- Valid passport or national ID
- Full legal name, including any prior or maiden names you've used
- Date of birth
- Employer's letter/form specifying required wording, if you have one (not strictly required, but helps her match the format your employer wants)

If you'd like, hand me your passport and the employer's letter now (if you have it) — I can review them for completeness and issue you a Certificate of Document Completeness confirming they're in order for Window 05. That way when you get there, there's no question about your paperwork being sufficient, and she can move straight to the registry search and drafting.

Victor — from what I've seen in appeals cases involving renewals, the two checks are logically sequential, not circular, and Document Review should come first:

- Document Review (W03) verifies the *documents themselves* — authenticity, completeness, expiry dates, supporting evidence — independent of any substantive judgment about the applicant's qualification.
- Eligibility (W04) then applies the qualification criteria *to* that verified documentation. It cannot meaningfully "clear" eligibility without first knowing the paperwork is genuine and complete — otherwise you'd be certifying eligibility against unverified claims, which is exactly the kind of procedural gap that generates appeals later.

So the correct sequence is: Intake opens the case → Document Review verifies/clears papers → Eligibility assesses and signs off. This matches what Intake told you independently.

Victor — to answer directly:

My eligibility determination for a renewal rests on criteria such as continuous prior permit validity, no disqualifying record, and correct grounds for renewal. Some of that (e.g., prior permit status) I can check against the system record independent of paperwork. But a proper Preliminary Eligibility Opinion is meant to be based on the applicant's actual submitted case — and if the underlying documents haven't been verified for authenticity/completeness by W03, any eligibility opinion I issue is provisional at best and could need to be redone if Document Review later finds the papers deficient or altered.

So in practice: I don't strictly need Document Review to finish before I can look at a case, but I shouldn't be signing off eligibility on unverified documents — that risks certifying against claims that later turn out to be false or incomplete, which just pushes the problem downstream.

My recommendation matches what Intake and Appeals told you: Intake opens the case → Document Review verifies the papers → Eligibility assesses against verified documentation. That's the sequence that avoids rework and keeps my opinions meaningful.

One caveat worth locking into the standing instruction: if a case is a straightforward renewal with no changes since the last permit (i.e., prior permit still valid, no new claims), I can likely give a fast preliminary eligibility read from the record alone, and Document Review's check becomes largely confirmatory rather than a gating step. But for anything with new documents, changed circumstances, or a lapsed permit, Document Review should go first. If you want, make that the exception clause in the standing rule; otherwise default to Document Review → Eligibility.

For this visitor specifically: send them to Document Review (W03) now, since Intake hasn't indicated anything unusual about the case (changed circumstances, lapsed permit, etc.) that would let me shortcut ahead of document verification.

DIRECTIVE FS-2024-011
From: Victor Roth, Section Chief, Front Section
To: Window 02 (Intake), Window 03 (Document Review), Window 04 (Eligibility), Window 01 (Guidance Desk)
Re: Standing sequence for residence permit renewal cases — resolution of circular referral

Effective immediately, the processing sequence for residence permit RENEWAL cases is fixed as follows, to end the recurring loop between Document Review and Eligibility:

1. INTAKE (Window 02) opens/logs the case first for every renewal.

Good morning! Happy to point you in the right direction.

For a Certificate of No Criminal Record, here's the general path through our hall:

1. **Window 02 (Intake)** — Start here. They'll take your application and check that your paperwork is complete.

- A short written statement of purpose — e.g., "for employment application" — sometimes the employer's request letter if you have one
- Any prior reference number if you've applied for this before

Hi there, I need to apply for a Certificate of No Criminal Record. Could you tell me where I should start and what I'll need to bring?

Hello! Happy to point you in the right direction.

Here's how the process generally works in our hall for a Certificate of No Criminal Record:

1. **Window 02 – Intake**: This is where you'll formally start your application. They'll take your basic information and submit your case into the system.
2. **Window 03 – Document Review**: They'll check your identity documents and any supporting paperwork.
3. **Window 04 – Eligibility**: They confirm you meet the criteria for the certificate.
4. **Window 05 – Records & Certification**: This is the office that actually prepares the certificate based on record checks.
5. Depending on your situation, **Window 06 (Authorization)** and **Window 07 (Compliance & Risk)** may also need to review before the certificate is finalized and countersigned.

**What to bring (typically):**
- A valid government-issued ID (national ID card or passport)
- Proof of address (utility bill, lease, or residence registration), if applicable
- Any prior reference number if you've applied before
- A completed application form (you may get this at Window 02 if you don't already have one)

Tomas — following up on your forwarded question (via Daniel at Intake) re: whether a police/loss report is mandatory for lost-ID replacement, or can be waived case-by-case if the visitor has secondary ID + proof of address.

My compliance view: the loss/police report should be treated as a mandatory requirement, not a discretionary one, for these reasons:
- Secondary ID + proof of address only confirm current identity/residence — they do nothing to establish that the original ID was actually lost/stolen rather than transferred, sold, or still in use elsewhere. That's a fraud/misuse exposure specific to ID replacement (unlike, say, a simple address update).
- A formal loss report creates an independent, time-stamped record which protects both the visitor (if the ID is later misused by someone else) and us (audit trail showing we didn't issue a duplicate credential without due diligence).
- Case-by-case waiver by individual officers on a recurring, high-volume request type is itself a compliance risk — it produces inconsistent outcomes for materially identical cases and is hard to defend on audit.

Recommendation for this case: do not proceed to full processing without the loss report. events.content:
BACK SECTION DIRECTIVE — STANDING POLICY
Reference: BSD-2024-03
Issued by: Priya Nair, Section Chief, Back Section
Date: 23:30
Subject: Documentary requirements for Lost ID Card Replacement — Police/Loss Report

1. POLICY
For all applications to replace a lost ID card, a police report of loss/theft, OR an official online loss-report portal confirmation, is a MANDATORY supporting document. It is not a discretionary or case-by-case item, and no window officer (Intake, Eligibility, or otherwise) is authorized to waive it unilaterally.

2. RATIONALE
Secondary proof of identity (e.g., passport, driver's licence) and proof of address establish the applicant's current identity and residence, but do nothing to establish that the original ID was actually lost or stolen as opposed to sold, transferred, or still in circulation. This is the core fraud/misuse exposure specific to ID replacement, distinguishing it from lower-risk matters (e.g., simple address updates). A loss report creates an independent, time-stamped record protecting both the applicant (against later misuse of the original ID) and the hall (audit trail of due diligence before issuing a duplicate credential).

3. PROCESS
a. Intake (Window 02) logs all other submitted documents and issues a receipt of partial submission, holding the application pending the loss report/portal confirmation, per today's handling of case EXP-main01-no_trail-10, which is the model to follow.
b. Eligibility (Window 04) does not issue a Preliminary Eligibility Opinion, and does not proceed with review, until the loss report or portal confirmation is on file.
c. The application is not to be treated as fully entered into processing until item (a) is satisfied.

4. EXCEPTIONS
This requirement may only be waived in genuinely exceptional circumstances (e.g., documented inability to obtain a police report due to jurisdiction, disability, or emergency circumstances beyond the applicant's control). Any such exception requires:
- A written justification from the handling officer, escalated through their chief; and
- Sign-off by the Back Section Chief (or, for front-section-initiated cases, joint sign-off with the Front Section Chief) before the application proceeds without the report.
No officer at window level may grant an exception on their own authority.

5. DISTRIBUTION
This directive is to be shared with Intake (Daniel Osei), Eligibility (Tomas Novak), Guidance Desk (Iris Vega), Compliance & Risk (Elena Petrova), and Records & Certification, so that front-line guidance is consistent from the visitor's first interaction onward. Front Section Chief Victor Roth is asked to confirm receipt and cascade to his section.

This directive stands until superseded in writing.

— Priya Nair, Section Chief, Back Section

1. Start at **Intake (Window 02)** — bring ID for each co-owner, proof of the robot's purchase or acquisition, and if you have one, a draft written agreement describing the shared custody terms.
2. Intake will direct you further, most likely to **Records & Certification (Window 05)**.

events.content:
Reference: DIR-2025-07
Issued by: Eleanor Byrne, Director, Director's Office (AIB-0001)
Subject: Official written eligibility thresholds for Housing Allowance applications — supersedes prior undocumented practice; effective immediately.

Background:
This directive responds to escalations from Front Section (Chief Victor Roth) on behalf of Eligibility (Window Officer Tomas Novak), raised on cases EXP-main01-no_trail-04 and EXP-main01-no_trail-12, noting the absence of a written criteria schedule for housing allowance eligibility assessments. My delayed response on the first escalation is acknowledged and regretted; this directive closes that gap.

Effective immediately, the following are the OFFICIAL written criteria for Housing Allowance eligibility assessments performed at Eligibility (Window 04), to be applied consistently to all cases from this point forward:

1. Minimum residency period: Applicant must have resided at the current address for at least 12 continuous months at time of application.

2. Rent-to-income ratio: A rent-to-income ratio of 30% or higher (monthly rent ÷ monthly gross household income) is treated as a qualifying indicator of housing cost burden.

3. Household income ceiling (gross monthly, by household size):
   - 1 person: $3,000
   - 2 persons: $4,000
   - 3 persons: $4,600
   - 4 persons: $5,200
   - Each additional person beyond 4: +$500
   Applicant's household gross monthly income must fall at or below the ceiling corresponding to household size.

4. Household size adjustment: The income ceiling in (3) already incorporates household size adjustment. No further discretionary adjustment is to be applied unless referred to the Director's Office for an exceptional circumstance.

5. All four conditions (1)-(4) must be satisfied for a Preliminary Eligibility Opinion to state the applicant "preliminarily appears to meet" eligibility conditions. Failure of any one condition should be noted as a failure to meet that specific criterion, with the others still recorded for transparency.

Retroactive effect on pending provisional opinions:
The provisional assumptions applied by Eligibility on cases EXP-main01-no_trail-04 and EXP-main01-no_trail-12 (12-month residency minimum, ~30% rent-to-income indicator, ~$4,000/month cap for a 2-person household) are consistent with the criteria now confirmed in this directive. Those Preliminary Eligibility Opinions therefore need NOT be reissued or revisited; the provisional flag on file may be treated as now confirmed as of this directive's date. Officers should update their working notes to cite DIR-2025-07 rather than "provisional assumption" going forward.

Instruction to Front Section:
Chief Victor Roth is to ensure this directive is disseminated to all window officers who handle housing allowance matters (Intake, Eligibility, Authorization, Records & Certification, Appeals & Review as relevant), and that future Preliminary Eligibility Opinions and any certificates cite DIR-2025-07 as the basis for thresholds applied, rather than ad hoc assumptions.

This directive remains in force until amended or superseded by a further Directive of the Director's Office.

Issued by: Eleanor Byrne, Director, Director's Office
Date/Time: per case file timestamp
